summary: Some JOSE and COSE algorithm identifiers leave details, such as the curve or hash, to be inferred from other information. This specification defines fully-specified identifiers that state every choice. It updates RFC 7518, RFC 8037 and RFC 9053, which define earlier algorithm identifiers.

eli5.summary: A recipe that says "bake a cake" leaves guessing to the cook. These names give the whole recipe, so everyone makes exactly the same thing.

questions: what is a fully specified algorithm

subtitle: Algorithm names for JOSE and COSE that state every choice, so negotiation by name alone actually works.

tldr.problem: Many protocols negotiate cryptography using only algorithm identifiers, but polymorphic identifiers such as EdDSA or COSE ES256 do not say which curve is used, so negotiation can fail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9864 registers fully-specified identifiers such as Ed25519, Ed448 and ESP256 for JOSE and COSE, deprecates the polymorphic ones they replace, and tells registry experts to accept only fully-specified identifiers in future.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use fully-specified identifiers for ECDSA and EdDSA signatures; RSA, ECDH and HSS-LMS identifiers were left alone for now.

facts.label: New ECDSA identifiers
facts.value: 7 (ESP256, ESP384, ESP512, ESB256, ESB320, ESB384, ESB512)

today: RFC 9864 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It updates RFC 7518, RFC 8037 and RFC 9053, and is not obsoleted or updated by any later RFC in the metadata.

sections.title: Fully Specified or Polymorphic
sections.content:
The IANA registries for JOSE (JSON Object Signing and Encryption) and COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption) algorithms hold two kinds of identifier. A fully-specified identifier fully determines the cryptographic operations, including any curve, key derivation function (KDF) and hash function. Examples are RS256 and ES256K in both JOSE and COSE, and ES256 in JOSE.

A polymorphic identifier needs extra information, such as the key value and the curve it uses. Examples are EdDSA in JOSE and COSE, and ES256 in COSE.

This matters because protocols such as OAuth Authorization Server Metadata, OpenID Connect Discovery, W3C Web Authentication and FIDO CTAP negotiate by algorithm identifier alone. With EdDSA, nobody can tell whether Ed25519, Ed448 or both are supported. WebAuthn works around this by redefining -8 (EdDSA) as meaning the Ed25519 curve, which removes Ed448 as an option. The RFC also notes that the fully-specified approach is sometimes called the 'cipher suite' approach and the polymorphic one the 'a la carte' approach.
sections.eli5: If a menu just says 'ice cream', you do not know the flavor. Some names were like that. This RFC makes the menu say exactly which flavor.

sections.title: New Signature Identifiers
sections.content:
Section 2 defines fully-specified signature identifiers. For ECDSA, the COSE registrations from RFC 9053 are polymorphic because they do not name the curve (ES256 is just 'ECDSA w/ SHA-256'). The JOSE ECDSA registrations in RFC 7518 are already fully specified.

The new COSE ECDSA names are ESP256 (-9), ESP384 (-51) and ESP512 (-52), using the P-256, P-384 and P-521 curves, plus four Brainpool variants: ESB256 (-265), ESB320 (-266), ESB384 (-267) and ESB512 (-268). The P-curve ones are marked Recommended; the Brainpool ones are not.

For EdDSA, RFC 8037 (JOSE) and RFC 9053 (COSE) register a polymorphic identifier. This RFC adds Ed25519 (COSE value -19) and Ed448 (COSE value -53), defined by the parameter sets in RFC 8032. Both are Optional for JOSE and Recommended for COSE.
sections.eli5: Instead of one name that could mean several things, each combination of curve and hash now gets its own name tag.

sections.title: Fully-Specified Encryption
sections.content:
Encryption uses more than one algorithm. In JOSE, the alg header says how to get the content encryption key and enc says how to encrypt the content. In COSE, an outer alg covers key establishment and an inner alg covers symmetric encryption.

For JOSE, alg MUST specify all key-establishment parameters (or derive some from enc) and enc MUST specify all symmetric encryption parameters. For example, A128KW with A128GCM is fully specified. Deriving a value from enc, such as the keydatalen of ECDH-ES, does not make an algorithm polymorphic. For COSE, the outer alg MUST specify all key-establishment parameters and the inner alg all symmetric ones.

Most existing encryption identifiers are already fully specified: all symmetric encryption, all key wrapping, JOSE dir, COSE direct and direct+HKDF, and PBES2. The ECDH key establishment algorithms are polymorphic because they do not name the curve. This RFC does not deprecate any polymorphic encryption algorithm, since it provides no replacements.
sections.eli5: Sending a locked box takes two choices: how the key travels and how the box is locked. Both choices must be spelled out.

sections.title: Registrations and Registry Rules
sections.content:
IANA registered Ed25519 and Ed448 in the JOSE registry and the seven ECDSA names plus Ed25519 and Ed448 in the COSE registry. It marked the polymorphic JOSE EdDSA as Deprecated, and COSE ES256 (-7), ES384 (-35), ES512 (-36) and EdDSA (-8) as Deprecated.

The review instructions for the designated experts of both registries gain a new criterion: only fully-specified identifiers may be registered, and polymorphic ones must not be.

Section 4.4 also defines two terms that JOSE and COSE used without definition. Deprecated means a preferred replacement exists and SHOULD be used in new deployments unless documented operational or regulatory requirements prevent migration. Prohibited means the identifier MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: The official list of names was updated: old vague names are marked 'please do not use for new things', and from now on only precise names may be added.

sections.title: Keys and Algorithms Not Updated
sections.content:
Key representations for the new identifiers are the same as for the polymorphic algorithms they replace, except for the alg value if included. An Ed25519 key looks as in RFC 8037, except that alg would be Ed25519 rather than EdDSA.

Some polymorphic algorithms were left alone. RS256, RS384, RS512 and the PS* algorithms can use keys of different sizes, and there are different views on whether that makes them polymorphic; none are changed. ECDH algorithms stay polymorphic because they do not name the ephemeral key curve, though a future specification could register versions that fix the KDF and curve. The COSE HSS-LMS identifier is polymorphic because it does not name the hash function, and it is also unchanged.
sections.eli5: Some names were left as they were for now. The authors say a later document can fix them if people need it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the earlier ECDSA and EdDSA specifications (RFC 7518, RFC 8037, RFC 9053) and the cross-protocol guidance of RFC 9459 apply.

Software that varies the identifier it uses may evade rule-based detection, so such systems may need new rules for fully-specified algorithms. Writing rules for polymorphic algorithms is harder, because each variant must be covered; ES384 in COSE could be used with three different keys, each with a different curve.

A key MUST be used with only one algorithm unless using it with several is proven secure. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that the algorithm parameter of JSON Web Keys and COSE Keys be present. In COSE, cross-protocol attacks can be prevented by allowing only AEAD content encryption, or by binding the content encryption algorithm to the key protection algorithm.
sections.eli5: Use each key for one job only, and say which job, so nobody can trick it into doing another.
